paragraphs: Such increases in the market price may last as long as the government regulations which give rise to them.

The market price of any particular commodity may remain above its natural price for a long time, but it can seldom remain below it for long. If any part of it were paid below the natural rate, the people whose interests were affected would feel the loss immediately. They would at once withdraw some of the land, labour or capital used in that activity. The quantity brought to market would soon be no more than enough to supply the effectual demand, meaning the demand of those willing and able to pay. Its market price would therefore soon rise to the natural price, at least where there was perfect liberty.

Consider the statutes of apprenticeship and other corporation laws. When a manufacture is prospering, they allow a workman to raise his wages a good deal above their natural rate. Yet when it decays, the same laws sometimes oblige him to let them fall a good deal below it. In the first case they exclude many people from his employment; in the second, they exclude him from many employments.

The effect of such regulations, however, is far less lasting when it lowers wages than when it raises them. In one direction it may endure for many centuries. In the other, it can last no longer than the lives of some of the workmen who were bred to the business while it prospered. Once they are gone, the number of people trained in the trade will naturally adjust itself to the effectual demand. Only a policy as violent as that of Indostan or ancient Egypt could keep wages or the profits of stock below their natural rate in one employment for several generations. In those countries every man was bound by religion to follow his father's occupation, and changing it was considered the most horrid sacrilege.
This is all that I think necessary to note at present about how market prices deviate from natural prices, whether occasionally or permanently.

The natural price itself varies with the natural rate of each of its component parts, namely wages, profit and rent. In every society this rate varies according to its circumstances: according to its riches or poverty, and according to whether it is advancing, stationary or declining. In the four following chapters, I shall try to explain the causes of these different variations as fully and distinctly as I can.

First, I shall try to explain the circumstances which naturally determine the rate of wages. I shall also show how they are affected by the riches or poverty of the society, and by its advancing, stationary or declining state.
Secondly, I shall try to show the circumstances which naturally determine the rate of profit. I shall also show how similar variations in the state of the society affect them.
